title: Longest Run Found in Both Arrays
statement:
You get two integer arrays a and b. Find the longest block of values that appears contiguously in both arrays, in the same order, and return its length.

The block may start at different positions in the two arrays. Return 0 if the arrays share no value at all.

examples.why: [1, 2, 9] sits at the end of a and at the start of b. [4, 7] is shared too, but it is shorter.
1, 2, 3 appear in both in order, but not next to each other. No two neighbours in a are also neighbours in b.
The whole of b appears inside a.

hints: Fix a pair of starting positions i in a and j in b. How long does the match starting there last? Can you reuse that number for (i + 1, j + 1)?
Let len[i][j] be the length of the common block that ends at a[i - 1] and b[j - 1]. If those two values differ, it is 0.
If they are equal, len[i][j] = len[i − 1][j − 1] + 1. The answer is the largest entry. Only the previous row is needed.

explain.intuition:
A shared block is a pair of end positions, one in each array, plus a length. If the block ends at a[i − 1] and b[j − 1], then dropping its last value gives a shared block ending one step earlier in both arrays. So the longest block ending at (i, j) is one longer than the longest block ending at (i − 1, j − 1), or 0 when the two values differ.

This is the "longest common substring" table. It differs from the common-subsequence table in one place: on a mismatch the run resets to 0 instead of copying the best neighbour, because a gap breaks contiguity. Think of diffing two versions of a file and looking for the longest block of lines that moved unchanged.
steps: Make a row prev of m + 1 zeros for the previous value of i.
For each i from 1 to n, build cur: for each j, set cur[j] = prev[j − 1] + 1 if a[i − 1] === b[j − 1], else 0.
Swap rows and continue. Return the largest value.
pitfalls: Using the common-subsequence rule max(left, up) on a mismatch. That answers a different question; the second example returns 3 instead of 1.
Returning the last cell of the table. The best block can end anywhere, so take the maximum over all cells.
Updating a single row in place from left to right. cur[j] needs the old prev[j − 1], which a left-to-right pass has already overwritten. Go right to left or keep two rows.

solutions.title: Try every pair of starts
solutions.idea: For every start i in a and j in b, walk forward while the values match.

solutions.title: DP on block ends, two rows
solutions.idea: len[i][j] = len[i − 1][j − 1] + 1 when a[i − 1] equals b[j − 1], else 0. Keep only the previous row.

followups: With arrays of 100 000 values each, O(n · m) is too slow. How do binary search on the length plus rolling hashes get it near O((n + m) log n)?
Return the block itself, not just its length.
